setupSteps: Seat height: sit so the top of the pad sits snugly under your armpits and the back of the upper arms lie flat on the pad. Not so low that you shrug up, not so high that you lean over the pad (Legion, Workout Labs, BarBend). Feet flat on the floor.
Chest: a slight forward lean so the chest rests lightly against the pad (BarBend); do not hunch.
Pad check: the pad should not dig into the armpits; adjust the seat down one notch if it does.

Machine version: set the seat so the pad is at armpit level and the arms rest on it; set the handle start position so you can start with a slight bend; use the pin or T-handle on that machine (they differ; read the label or ask staff). Select a light weight first (Bodybuilding.com, Hoist manual, UWO equipment guide).
EZ-bar: put a light weight on the bar (start with the bar alone or about 5-10 kg total, est.) and fit collars. Rest the bar on the hooks if the bench has them.

Grip: underhand (palms up), about shoulder-width, hands on the angled sections that feel comfortable for the wrists (sources say shoulder-width, one says slightly wider); wrists straight, thumbs wrapped.
Get the bar off the hooks: ask staff or a partner to hand it to you the first few times, especially if heavy.
Dumbbell: one arm at a time, the back of the upper arm on the pad, free hand resting on the pad or your thigh.
Spotter: not needed for light weight; for heavier sets have a partner to hand the bar back.

steps.title: Sit and place the upper arms
steps.action: Sit with feet flat, tuck the armpits against the top of the pad and lay the back of both upper arms along it.
steps.feel: Upper arms supported, shoulders relaxed, not shrugged.
steps.visualCheck: Side: pad under the armpit, upper arm flat on the pad. Front: elbows level and the same distance apart.

steps.title: Take the bar
steps.action: Hold the bar underhand at about shoulder-width, thumbs wrapped, wrists straight; let a helper hand it over if needed.
steps.visualCheck: Side: wrists in line with forearms. Front: hands evenly spaced.

steps.title: Set the start position
steps.action: Lower the bar until the arms are almost straight, and stop just short of locking the elbows (a very slight bend remains).
steps.feel: Gentle stretch in the biceps, no pain at the elbow crease.
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbow slightly bent, upper arm still on the pad.

steps.title: Curl up
steps.action: Bend the elbows and bring the bar up in an arc toward the front of the shoulders, keeping the upper arms on the pad.
steps.feel: Biceps squeezing; shoulders and back quiet.
steps.visualCheck: Side: only the forearm moves; the elbow stays in place on the pad.

steps.title: Squeeze at the top
steps.action: Stop when the hands are in front of the shoulders; do not curl so far that the elbows lift off the pad.
steps.breathing: Keep breathing out or hold briefly, no long breath-hold.
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbow angle about 60 degrees or less (est.); armpits still on the pad.

steps.title: Lower slowly
steps.action: Lower the bar under control, taking at least as long as the lift; one source suggests 2-3 seconds.
steps.feel: Biceps lengthening under load; no drop at the end.
steps.visualCheck: Side: bar moves smoothly; elbows do not slide forward.

steps.title: Stop just short of lockout and repeat
steps.action: At the bottom keep a slight bend; do not let the weight snap the elbow straight.
steps.breathing: Breathe in, then out as you lift again.
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbow angle about 150 or more but under about 175 (est.).

steps.title: Finish and put the bar back
steps.action: After the last rep, hold the bar up and ask a helper to take it, or lower it to the hooks, then stand up.
steps.visualCheck: Bar on the hooks before you let go.

commonMistakes.title: Lifting the elbows off the pad
commonMistakes.text: Lifting the elbows off the pad. Why: the shoulder takes over and the pad cannot protect you; sources call it one of the most common preacher curl faults, especially with heavier weight. Fix: glue the upper arm to the pad from elbow to armpit and lower the weight if you cannot.

commonMistakes.title: Swinging or heaving the body
commonMistakes.text: Swinging or heaving the body. Why: momentum hides weak muscles and shifts load to the back and shoulders (one source ties this to ego lifting on the machine). Fix: lighter weight, chest on the pad, sit still.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping the weight at the bottom
commonMistakes.text: Dropping the weight at the bottom. Why: the biceps tendon is loaded at near-straight elbow positions during eccentric (lowering) work; the review quoted a heavy eccentric (68 kg or more) as a rupture situation; the 2008 case report describes a bilateral rupture on a preacher curl. Fix: lower for 2-3 seconds and never let the weight snap the elbow straight.

commonMistakes.title: Locking the elbow out at the bottom
commonMistakes.text: Locking the elbow out at the bottom. Why: the arm is loaded at its most stretched position; one coach and a PT-style source advise avoiding hyperextension. Fix: stop just short of straight.

commonMistakes.title: Going too heavy
commonMistakes.text: Going too heavy. Why: causes all of the above and can overtax the shoulder, elbow and wrist. Fix: pick a weight you can lower in 3 seconds for 10-12 reps with 2-3 reps in reserve (section 7).

commonMistakes.title: Seat too high or too low
commonMistakes.text: Seat too high or too low. Why: too low makes you shrug; too high makes you lean over the pad (Workout Labs). Fix: armpits at the top of the pad, upper arms flat.

commonMistakes.title: Uneven arms on the EZ-bar (stronger arm doing the work)
commonMistakes.text: Uneven arms on the EZ-bar (stronger arm doing the work). Why: one side lags (a trainer in the sources). Fix: switch to single-arm dumbbells or the machine and match reps.

commonMistakes.title: Bent wrists
commonMistakes.text: Bent wrists. Why: forearm strain. Fix: use the EZ-bar's angled sections and keep wrists straight.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: raises blood pressure briefly. Fix: breathe out as you curl.

commonMistakes.title: Using it every day
commonMistakes.text: Using it every day. Why: recovery. Fix: 2-3 sessions per week with a rest day between (est.).

safetyNotes: Biceps tendon (elbow): a 2008 case report describes bilateral distal biceps tendon rupture during a preacher curl; the distal tendon is most at risk during heavy lowering (68 kg or more in one review); the incidence is about 2.55 per 100,000 patient-years (one review). The risk comes from heavy, uncontrolled lowering rather than the exercise itself, but beginners should keep the weight light and lower slowly. Stop at once for a sudden pop, sharp pain or weakness at the elbow crease.

Elbow, wrist or shoulder history: one source advises skipping preacher variations with a history of injury, especially with heavy loads; a hammer-grip or cable curl is an alternative (hammer-style lowers wrist risk). See a physiotherapist for persistent pain.
High blood pressure: avoid breath-holding; stop 2-3 reps before failure.
Lower back pain: seated and supported, so usually fine; do not lean back or heave.
Pregnancy, recent surgery, osteoporosis, heart disease: see the table.
Spotter: not needed for light weight; ask for a hand-off of the bar for heavier sets and the first few times.
Equipment check: shake the bench, check the pad is secure and the seat pin is locked, check the bar collars and the machine pin.
Gym etiquette: wipe the pad and handles, rerack the bar and strip the weights, do not hog the bench between sets, do not film other members, ask staff before filming.
